chunks: My father (RA) narrated, saying: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi, from Abu Ubaydah al-Hadhdah, from Abu Ja'far (AS), who said: The Messenger of Allah (SAWW) said:

Allah, Great be His Glory, said: Verily, among My believing servants are those who strive in My worship. They rise from their sleep and the comfort of their pillows to perform supererogatory prayers during the nights and exhaust themselves in My worship. So I overpower them with sleep for a night or two, as a look-out by Me for them and to preserve them. They sleep until morning, and when they rise, they are disgusted with themselves and afflicted over it. And if I did not prevent them from doing what they desire of My worship, pride would enter them, and pride would lead them to destruction through their deeds and their satisfaction with themselves, until they think they have surpassed the worshippers, and they have exceeded the limit of inadequacy in their worship. Thus they become distant from Me at that time, while they think they are drawing close to Me.

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Inadequacy or falling short (of the ideal state)
key_terms.الْعَجَب: Pride or self-admiration in one's own deeds

ai.seo_question: Why does God make diligent worshippers fall asleep during night prayers?
ai.summary: In Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid*, this hadith qudsi illustrates the divine attribute of *al-Lutf* (gentleness) by showing how God intentionally induces sleep in the devout to curb *al-'ajab* (self-admiration), a subtle spiritual disease that can turn worship into a source of arrogance. This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the balance between *mujahadah* (striving) and *tawadu'* (humility), warning that excessive self-satisfaction distances the servant from God despite their apparent devotion.
